text:
On 3rd May 2019 the Cyclone Fani ('Foni'), a category 4 storm, impacted three states in India (Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and West Bengal). Odisha was the worst hit with more than 15 million people including 4.8 million children affected. Fani was untimely — one of the rarest summer cyclones, the first in 43 years and one of only 3 summer cyclones to hit Odisha in 150 years. 

The Government of Odisha coordinated one of the largest emergency preparedness exercises ever: more than 45,000 volunteers, 2,000 emergency workers, 100,000 officials, youth clubs, and other civil society organisations, along with NDRF, ODRAF, and Panchayati Raj Institutions, worked round the clock to evacuate 1.47 million people before forecasted landfall. This unprecedented mobilisation kept casualties low: 64 deaths reported and 160 injured (State Emergency Operation Centre, Bhubaneswar). The UN recognised this as a good practice for effective preparedness and early warning. 

Despite the success in avoiding higher death tolls, the cyclone severely affected lives and livelihoods of more than 28 million people across 3 states. 24 districts were affected across Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, and West Bengal. Severely impacted areas are all in Odisha, mainly Puri (landfall), Khurdha, Cuttack, Nayagarh and Jagatsinghpur.

The Extremely Severe Cyclonic Storm 'Fani' crossed the Odisha coast close to Puri between 0800 and 1000 hrs on 3 May 2019 with maximum wind speed of 175-180 kmph. The cyclone pummeled the coast with heavy rainfall and coastal flooding, affecting nearly 28 million people along its route. After hitting Puri the system moved to Khordha district with high wind and heavy rainfall including Bhubaneswar, before moving northwards to Cuttack. It then moved into Gangetic West Bengal as a Severe Cyclonic Storm (70-80 kmph) by early morning of 4 May. From West Bengal it moved further North-North-Eastwards and emerged into Bangladesh (60-70 kmph gusting to 80 kmph). By Sunday the cyclone had dissipated, but Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Manipur, Mizoram, Tripura and Nagaland witnessed moderate to heavy rainfall for over a week afterwards. 

Districts of Cuttack, Khordha, Bhubaneswar and Puri were severely affected with complete shutdown of power and telecommunications. Extensive damages to housing reported across most affected districts. Roughly 40% of trees were uprooted, disrupting road communication. Summer crops, orchards, and plantations were devastated at large scale. 14 districts (159 blocks, 52 urban local bodies, 18,168 villages) were affected in Odisha: Angul, Balasore, Bhadrak, Cuttack, Dhenkanal, Ganjam, Jagatsinghpur, Jajpur, Kendrapara, Keonjhar, Khordha, Mayurbhanj, Nayagarh, Puri. 508,467 houses reported damaged (as of 7 May 2019). Livestock casualties: 3.45 million (narrative) / 3.73 million (sidebar). 5,244 primary and 1,547 secondary school buildings damaged.

Per the State Emergency Operation Centre, West Bengal, there were no casualties or major damage in the districts through which the cyclone passed. People returned from relief shelters; all relief centres closed on Monday, 6 May 2019. 

However, while Andhra Pradesh and West Bengal returned to normalcy quickly, the situation in Odisha remained fluid even after 9 days due to complete breakdown of communications, roads, and electricity. Relief teams faced challenges providing food, medicine, and drinking water to affected households; many areas remained inaccessible due to telecom and road disruptions. In Puri, which bore the brunt of the storm, debris of damaged houses and tree branches littered the streets; relief teams worked on a war footing to clear streets, but several interior roads remained blocked. Acute shortages of drinking water and food were reported from several areas.

metadata.section_title: Post-event status by state (as of 12 May 2019)

text:
Humanitarian Leadership and Coordination — National Level. The Government of India and the respective state governments took the lead in coordinating rescue and relief. Humanitarian organisations undertook a Joint Rapid Needs Assessment (JRNA) while pitching in with immediate relief. UNICEF worked with the Government, sectoral departments, and humanitarian organisations to monitor the situation for children and coordinate initial assessments with the NGO Inter-Agency Group (IAG) in the most affected districts. 

On Monday 6 May 2019, Prime Minister Narendra Modi conducted an aerial survey of cyclone damage. He announced an additional central assistance of ₹10,000 million (US$142.81 million) on top of ₹3,408.75 million (US$48.09 million) already announced. From the PM National Relief Fund he announced ex-gratia of ₹200,000 per next-of-kin of the deceased and ₹50,000 per seriously injured person. 

The National Crisis Management Committee (NCMC), chaired by the Cabinet Secretary, held daily meetings with the states and Central Ministries. The Ministry of Home Affairs maintained constant contact with State Chief Secretaries and relief commissioners. A combined ₹10,860 million (US$153 million) was released in advance from the State Disaster Response Fund (SDRF) to Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Tamil Nadu, and West Bengal.

metadata.section_title: Humanitarian Leadership and Coordination — National Level

text:
Andhra Pradesh preparedness and response. The Chief Minister's Office directly supervised preparedness. The Andhra Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority (APSDMA) led response through district collectors. The State Government designated 3 IAS officers, 15 Special Officers and 38 Mandal level officers to supervise rescue and relief. Trained Self-Help Group members under the UNICEF-APSDMA-DRR programmes, along with CADME (UNICEF partner), participated. Save the Children Fund, Caritas India, and Plan India conducted rapid assessments through local partners. UNICEF and partners in support of GoAP focused on service provision through line departments. 

Impact in AP: 4 Mandals, 145 villages of Srikakulam district severely affected. 29 schools reported damaged. About 304 houses in 6 Mandals fully damaged. Srikakulam hit by wind speeds of 140 kmph. 733 villages across 3 districts (Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, Vishakhapatnam) affected. 

State Response (AP): 120 Relief Camps established at cyclone shelters, schools, and office buildings with food, drinking water, generators, and medical assistance through ANMs. 300 NDRF members deployed — Srikakulam (225), Vizianagaram (25), Vishakhapatnam (50).

West Bengal preparedness and response. The state reported minor losses and damages. 1,985 kutcha houses partially damaged due to heavy rain and strong winds. About 24,642 persons evacuated and relocated to 471 relief camps. Affected districts returned to normalcy by 5 May 2019 and all relocated people returned home. The state government issued communications to all Government Departments for damage reporting; Fani-affected districts were asked to submit detailed house-damage enumerations for House Damage Assistance as per SDRF/NDRF norms. The Central Government released ₹235.50 Crore to West Bengal in advance. 

State Response (WB): Under the Chief Secretary's leadership, preparedness was reviewed with all key line departments and armed forces including NDRF, Kolkata Police, Indian Navy, and Army. PWD, PHED, Health & Family Welfare, Irrigation, Power, and Fisheries departments operated 24-hour control rooms. Affected districts: Kolkata, East and West Medinipur, Jhargram, South and North 24 Parganas, Howrah, Hooghly.

Odisha preparedness. In what could be considered the biggest preparedness mobilisation, more than 45,000 volunteers, 2,000 emergency workers, 100,000 officials, youth clubs, civil society organisations, NDRF, ODRAF, and Panchayati Raj Institutions teamed up the day before expected landfall to work around the clock to evacuate 1.34 million people and place them in 9,000 temporary shelters well before landfall. (Note: other sections cite 1.47 million as the final evacuated total.) 

Medical preparedness: the Government opened 703 Medical Relief Camps and deployed 199 Mobile Medical Teams. 1,945 pregnant women were shifted to Maa Gruhas (delivery points). About 9,482 open water sources were disinfected and 2,854,947 ORS sachets were distributed. 

Normal water supplies were restored in affected Urban Local Bodies except Konark, Puri, and Nimapara (Puri district); Jatni, Khordha, and Bhubaneswar (Khordha district); and Cuttack Municipal Corporation. In these ULBs, 339 tankers, 214 DG sets, and 1,029 PVC tanks were deployed to ensure water supply.

Odisha response. 20 teams of Odisha Disaster Rapid Action Force (ODRAF) and 525 fire teams were deployed. 14,70,197 persons (1.47 million) in 18 districts were evacuated and sheltered in 9,000 safe shelters. Free kitchens were opened to provide cooked food. 24,889 tourists were moved to safe places from Puri, Ganjam, Cuttack, and Balasore districts. Nearly 0.45 million polythene sheets (temporary shelter materials) were pre-positioned at district/sub-district levels, with 1.5 lakh kept in buffer stock at state headquarters. 100,000 food packets were prepared and kept ready for air dropping if required. 

Early warning and alerting: Cyclone-related alerts and suggested actions were delivered through Location Based Alert System (LBAS) SMS to 18 million subscribers residing in likely-affected areas. Cyclone warnings were disseminated through siren towers installed in coastal areas under the EWDS (automatic Coastal Warning System) project. Power distribution in Bhubaneswar City was expected to be fully restored within two days of the SitRep date.

metadata.section_title: Odisha — State Response (evacuation, shelters, early warning)

text:
Special Relief Package (Odisha). Households in 'extremely severely affected' districts (Puri, parts of Khurdha) received 50 kg rice, ₹2,000, and a polythene sheet. Households in 'severely affected' Khurdha received an additional one-month quota of rice, ₹1,000, and a polythene sheet. Households in 'moderately affected' Cuttack, Kendrapada, and Jagatsinghpur received ₹500 and an additional one-month rice quota. All affected districts: one month of additional pension to all pensioners. House building assistance per relief code: ₹95,100 for fully damaged structures, ₹5,200 for partially damaged, ₹3,200 for minor damages. Fully damaged houses will be reconstructed under existing housing schemes. 

The Women & Child Development Department issued instructions to Collectors covering: nutritional needs of children (6 months to 6 years), pregnant and lactating mothers; protocols for women and children in cyclone centres and relief camps; early resumption of Anganwadi centres; reporting damage to infrastructure; assessment of damage to food grains; vigilance against trafficking of women/adolescent girls; and timely payment to MAMATA scheme beneficiaries. 2,653 severely underweight and SAM children and 73,761 pregnant women were provided Take-Home Ration in advance. 104 SAM children were identified and 49 referred to Nutrition Rehabilitation Centres. Additional doctors were deployed to Bhadrak, Jagatsinghpur, Kendrapada, and Puri. 270 Mobile Medical Teams deployed; 1,945 pregnant women shifted to Maa Gruhas. Of 223 Cold Chain points in five districts, 172 were functional (running on DG sets).

metadata.section_title: Odisha — Special Relief Package & WCD directives

text: UN Hub in Bhubaneswar. A UN hub was set up temporarily in a hotel (until office functionality was fully restored) to coordinate and facilitate response by the UN and partners. UNICEF facilitated the establishment of the UN hub with other UN agencies. A meeting with the Special Officer for External Agency Coordination was held to discuss UN support and current IAG response.

UNICEF Actions — Andhra Pradesh. UNICEF Hyderabad continually monitored the situation with APSDMA and other partners. The DRR Officer conducted an initial assessment with special focus on children's vulnerability, psycho-social strategies, and identification of immediate community needs. UNICEF engaged CADME and the state IAG for initial assessment. 

UNICEF Actions — West Bengal. UNICEF Kolkata continually monitored the situation with Government counterparts, State IAG, and WHO. NGO partners were briefed on Core Commitments for Children (CCC) through a State IAG meeting on 2 May and on specific advisories from line departments. A booklet of key messages (WASH & C4D) on storm/flood response was shared with partners, state departments, and CSO partners. UNICEF shared key messages on Child Protection & Nutrition in Emergencies with IAG and NGO partners directly dealing with the cyclone emergency.

metadata.section_title: UNICEF Actions — Andhra Pradesh and West Bengal

text:
UNICEF Actions — Odisha (Coordination). The Chief Minister's Office requested UNICEF to support needs assessment and documentation of the state government's response to Cyclone Fani. The Odisha State Disaster Management Authority (OSDMA) requested, through the UN Resident Coordinator, a Joint Rapid Needs Assessment by the World Bank. Supported by UNICEF, the Inter-Agency Group (IAG) carried out a Joint Rapid Needs Assessment (JRNA). 

UN agencies and NGOs met jointly with the Special Officer, Government of Odisha for External Agency Coordination to assure UN and IAG support. The Government decided to provide tarpaulin, solar LED lights/torches, sleeping mats, and WASH items which may also be donated directly by NGOs. NGOs were requested to extend support for immediate response and recovery in five blocks of Puri district that were most impacted: Puri Sadar, Pipli, Satapada, Kanas, and Satyabadi. The IAG (including UNICEF) shared a unified response matrix ('3W') and an overall plan to cover 65,000 households. The Government activated NGO coordination cells in Puri and Khurdha districts and deputed two officials to coordinate the humanitarian response. UNICEF is supporting GO-NGO coordination in Puri, Khurdha, Jagatsinghpur, and Kendrapada through the state IAG.

UNICEF Actions — Odisha (Nutrition and Child Protection). In response to the order issued by the Women & Child Development Department, three UNICEF consultants were deployed to Jagatsinghpur, Gajapati and Ganjam, and Khurdha districts. The consultants are supporting damage assessment and early resumption of the Supplementary Nutrition Programme and other Integrated Child Development Scheme (ICDS) activities in all Anganwadi Centres (Early Childhood Centres). In Khurdha, the consultant is ensuring commencement of Take-Home Ration (THR) supply. 

Child Protection: It was decided to provide psychosocial counselling to all affected children in affected areas. As schools were closed for summer vacation, psychosocial counselling activity was planned to begin after schools reopen in June. UNICEF, along with the W&CD Department, started training for volunteers and teachers on psychosocial counselling.

UNICEF Actions — Odisha (Health and WASH). Health: UNICEF consultants supporting the Centre of Excellence at the State Institute of Health and Family Welfare were deputed to assist government in health promotion and communication. UNICEF proposed partnership for community awareness on handwashing, breastfeeding, supplementary nutrition, hygiene, and immunisations. 

WASH: Puri district had achieved Individual Household Latrine (IHHL) coverage of 81% pre-cyclone; Khurdha 86%. During the cyclone, household toilets were extensively damaged; restoration or rebuilding is expected to take time. UNICEF will support retrofitting of toilets, awareness generation, and capacity building in affected areas on water safety and security measures, menstrual hygiene management, and other hygiene issues.

JRNA finding (WASH). The cyclone affected water and sanitation across all assessed districts. Source contamination, water scarcity, and inadequate drinking water are major concerns. Pipe Water Supply (PWS) systems are defunct in all villages, largely due to power-supply disruptions. Most shelters do not have water storage facility. Most individual household toilets have suffered damages to various extent. Toilet use has substantially decreased due to poor condition and unavailability of water. Open defecation has increased. Assessed districts: Puri, Khordha, Jagatsinghpur, Cuttack.

JRNA finding (Shelter). Providing immediate shelter is a major concern due to extensive housing damage. Displaced occupants have taken shelter in cyclone/flood shelters, temporary shelters, neighbours' houses, relatives' places, or dismal makeshift arrangements. Almost 78% of houses in rural Puri district are fully or significantly damaged. Nearly 70% of houses in slum areas of Puri and Bhubaneswar cities are fully or damaged beyond repair. All kutcha houses were found fully or significantly damaged in Brahmagiri, Puri Sadar, Gop, and Nimapada blocks (Puri district), and in Khordha, Jagatsinghpur, and Cuttack districts. About 60% of pucca houses have a kutcha portion (e.g., kitchen); such kutcha portions were fully damaged in Puri and partly damaged in Jagatsinghpur, Khordha, and Cuttack. Occupants of all cyclone/temporary shelters complained of inadequate food supply — in Jagatsinghpur food was provided only on 5 May; in Puri only on 4 May.

JRNA finding (Food and Nutrition). Food availability has been seriously hampered by loss of cooking utensils, loss of food stock, market closures, and supply disruptions. Prices of essential items have risen, further limiting access to food grains, vegetables, and fruits. Significant damage to standing and harvested crops; short-term shortage of food grains expected in local markets. Large numbers of children do not have access to adequate nutritious food — food distribution reached some panchayats only on the third day, and some urban slums in Bhubaneswar only on 3 May. All assessed village households reported significant reduction in food intake. About 40% of rural households and 70% of slum households in Puri, Bhubaneswar, and Cuttack cities have no food stock left. Loss of stored materials, unavailability of water and power, rising prices, and supply-chain disruptions all compound reduced food availability.

JRNA finding (Education). As the summer vacation had begun, education was not expected to be affected in the short term. However, extensive damages to school infrastructure and teaching/learning materials were reported. Students of poor households with kutcha houses lost books, notebooks, study materials, and uniforms — mostly affecting higher classes. Some students' cycles were damaged, though such losses are not very extensive. Since schools are closed, Mid Day Meal (MDM) supply is discontinued, depriving students of at least one nutritious meal per day.

JRNA finding (Health). Due to complete breakdown in road and communication networks, access to immediate healthcare is a major challenge — an overall 60% decline in healthcare access was reported, attributed to lack of health camps and damage to health centres. Water contamination concerns are rising as water is drawn from open wells. Almost all pregnant women have been shifted to hospitals or delivery points — a commendable achievement. Most District, PHC, and CHC centres are not fully functional owing to non-availability of electricity or infrastructure damage. Puri district headquarter hospital building sustained damages but patient care was not affected. Regular vaccination has been disrupted; mobile health services hugely affected due to road obstruction. Health vulnerabilities of women have increased, and the assessment did not find any support tailored to women's special needs. Heatwave conditions have set in and are likely to intensify — implementation of the existing heatwave action plan is of prime importance.

JRNA finding (Protection). Men, women, and children are staying together in temporary or permanent shelters without enough privacy. Daily food intake by women has drastically decreased as available food is often apportioned to children and working males first. Domestic violence appears to be increasing due to heavy alcohol consumption (to be verified). Women feel more vulnerable due to lack of lighting and loss of secured dwellings. Children staying in shelters and in the open have become more vulnerable.

Immediate Humanitarian Needs — Heatwave and WASH. 

(1) Heatwave: Heatwave conditions have set in and are expected to intensify. More than 1 million persons including children will be exposed, compounded by loss of tree cover, extensive house damage, scarcity of drinking water, and shortage of food and medical supplies. Preventive measures are urgent. 

(2) WASH: Immediate priority is ensuring adequate water for drinking, household use, and livestock. Source contamination is reported across districts; chlorination of contaminated sources and supply of halogen tablets is needed on a war footing. Water storage tanks should be made available at Anganwadis, Primary Health Centres, temporary shelters, and at household level where families have lost water storage containers. Repair of toilets or construction of temporary toilets is needed, along with special hygiene awareness for children, adolescent girls, and women. Dignity kits for women are another major requirement.

Immediate Humanitarian Needs — Health, Education, Protection, Shelter, Food & Nutrition. 

(3) Health: Adequate supply of glucose, ORS, and clean water to all health facilities; mobile health camps; clean drinking water at public places; repair and renovation of hospitals and medical centres. 

(4) Education: Start Mid-Day Meal in schools in all affected areas; supply of books and study materials lost during the cyclone (mostly for secondary and higher students); assess school damages and ensure early repair of damaged buildings. 

(5) Protection: Provision of cubicles for women and adolescent girls for privacy during bathing and menstrual hygiene; Child Friendly Spaces to ensure child protection; lighting arrangements in camps and villages at night to ensure safety of girls, women, and elderly. 

(6) Shelter: Immediate supply of shelter kits, lighting solutions, utensils, stoves, and financial support to households that have lost houses totally or partly. Run regular and temporary shelters for at least 15 days with food supply. Support to rebuild/repair houses is a priority. 

(7) Food and Nutrition: Many poor daily-wage households have lost income — food and food materials needed to enable them to focus on repair and reconstruction. Mid-Day Meal should be started in affected areas so that children have at least one nutritious meal a day during the summer vacation school closure.

text:
National level UNICEF response and Way Forward. At national level, the UNICEF India Country Office Emergency Management Team met on 4 May and reconvened on 8 May. The UN Disaster Management Team (UNDMT) convened on 5 May and again on 10 May. The UNICEF Representative in her capacity as UN RC a.i. wrote to the State Government of Odisha to express solidarity and the UN's commitment to support. Delhi-based DRR and Outcome Sections have been providing support to State Offices with practical tools for preparedness ahead of landfall and for the UNICEF response. UNICEF, ONE UN, DRM practitioners, and NGO WhatsApp groups facilitate information exchange and coordination in the absence of a formal cluster system in India. UNICEF submitted a request for Emergency Funding. The UN will attend a meeting of the Department for Economic Affairs to discuss the possibility of a Joint Rapid Disaster Assessment (World Bank process) and a PDNA. First emergency Programme Cooperation Agreements are being finalised. 

Way forward. Andhra Pradesh and West Bengal are rapidly returning to normalcy. An improved understanding of damage and loss in Odisha is now available as the JRNA is completed. UNICEF will continue to focus on achieving the Core Commitments for Children in Humanitarian Action — strengthening inter-agency coordination, enabling children and women to access life-saving interventions, equitable access to essential health services, and behaviour-change communication. 

UNDMT is considering: (1) Developing a UN Coordinated Response Plan; (2) Mobilising resources through CERF based on rapid assessment of immediate lifesaving needs; (3) Supporting Detailed Assessment / PDNA if requested by the State Government.
